la:verb:reicio.gloss: to throw, cast or fling back
senses: to throw, cast or fling back
to chase, force or drive back, repel
to throw or cast oneself back or again; throw or fling oneself anywhere
to cast off, repel, remove, reject, repulse; deter, divert
to refuse, reject, scorn, disdain, despise
to refer, remand or hand over to
to put off to a later time, defer, postpone, delay
la:verb:reicio.html:
rē-ĭcĭo (better than rē-jĭcĭo), rejēci, jectum, 3 (reicis, dissyl., ;
and likewise reice,; and perh. also,; scanned elsewhere throughout rēĭcio, etc.), v. a.
jacio
, to throw, cast, or fling back (freq. and class.; cf.: remitto, retorqueo).
Lit.
In gen.
Of inanim. objects: imago nostros oculos rejecta revisit,; ; cf. : telum in hostes,: tunicam reicere, i. e. to fling back, fling over the shoulder (whereas abicere is to throw off, ), Lucil. ap. Müll.; cf.: togam in umerum,; : togam a sinistro,: togam ab umero,: amictum ex umeris,: ex umeris' vestem,: de corpore vestem,: penulam,; Burm.: sagulum,; : amictum, (3, 17), 13: vestem,: ab ore colubras,: capillum circum caput neglegenter,: manibus ad tergum rejectis, thrown back or behind, Asin. Pol. ap. : manus post terga,: scutum, to throw over one's back (in flight), ; Galb. ap. : parmas,: ut janua in publicum reiceretur,might be thrown back,: fatigata membra rejecit,i. e. stretched on the ground,: voluit ... Reicere Alcides a se mea pectora,to push back,: librum e gremio suo,to fling away,: sanguinem ore,to cast up, vomit,; so, sanguinem,; : bilem,: vinum,: aliquid ab stomacho,.— Poet.: oculos Rutulorum reicit arvis,turns away, averts,: pars (vocum) solidis adlisa locis rejecta sonorem Reddit,echoed,.—
Of living objects, to drive back, chase back, force back, repel (so in gen. not found in class. prose authors): hominem,: aliquem,: in bubilem reicere (boves),: pascentes a flumine capellas,: in postremam aciem,to place in the rear,.—
Reicere se, to throw or cast one's self back or again; or, in gen., to throw or fling one's self anywhere: tum illa Rejecit se in eum,flung herself into his arms,: se in gremium tuom,: se in grabatum,; cf.: in cubile rejectus est,; cf.: fatigata membra rejecit,leaned back,.—
In partic.
Milit. t. t., to force back, beat back, repel, repulse the enemy (cf.: repello, reprimo, refuto): eos, qui eruptionem fecerant, in urbem reiciebant,: reliqui in oppidum rejecti sunt,; fin.: Tusci rejecti armis,: ab Antiocheā hostem,; cf.: praesidia adversariorum Calydone, (where, however, as , the MSS. vacillate between rejecti and dejecti; v. Oud. N. cr.).—
Nautical t. t.: reici, to be driven back by a storm (while deferri or deici signifies to be cast away, and eici to be thrown on the shore, stranded; v. Drak.): naves tempestate rejectas eodem, unde erant profectae, revertisse, ; so, naves,: a Leucopetrā profectus ... rejectus sum austro vehementi ad eandem Leucopetram,; cf. ; : sin reflantibus ventis reiciemur,; .
Trop.
In gen., to cast off, remove, repel, reject: abs te socordiam omnem reice,: abs te religionem, Att. ap. Müll. (Trag. Rel. v. 430 Rib.): quam ut a nobis ratio verissima longe reiciat,: (hanc proscriptionem) nisi hoc judicio a vobis reicitis et aspernamini,: ab his reicientur plagae balistarum,: foedum contactum a casto corpore,; : ferrum et audaciam,; cf. ictus,; and: minas Hannibalis retrorsum,: (in Verrinis) facilius quod reici quam quod adici possit invenient,.—
In partic.
Pregn., to reject contemptuously; to refuse, scorn, disdain, despise; esp. of a lover, etc.: forsitan nos reiciat,: petentem,: Lydiam,: Socratem omnem istam disputationem rejecisse et tantum de vitā et moribus solitum esse quaerere,: refutetur ac reiciatur ille clamor,: qui Ennii Medeam spernat aut reiciat,; of an appeal to the Senate: quae cum rejecta relatio esset,: recens dolor consolationes reicit ac refugit,: ad bona deligenda et reicienda contraria,; cf. (vulgares reïce taedas, deligere),: rejectā praedā,: condiciones, Auct. B. Alex. 39: rejecit dona nocentium,.—
In jurid. lang.: judices reicere, to set aside, challenge peremptorily, reject the judges appointed by lot: cum ex CXXV. judicibus quinque et LXX. reus reiceret,; ; ; ; ; ; 2, 3, 59, § 146; ; .—
In the philosoph. lang. of the Stoics: reicienda and rejecta (as a transl. of the Gr. ἀποπροηγμένα), rejectable things, i. e. evils to be rejected, ; ; ; cf. rejectaneus.—
With a designation of the term. ad quem, to refer to, make over to, remand to: ad ipsam te epistulam reicio,: in hunc gregem vos Sullam reicietis? (with transferre).—
Publicists' t. t.: reicere aliquid or aliquem ad senatum (consules, populum, pontifices, etc.), to refer a matter, or the one whom it concerns, from one's self to some other officer or authorized body (esp. freq. in Liv.; v. the passages in Drak.): totam rem ad Pompeium,: senatus a se rem ad populum rejecit,; cf.: ab tribunis ad senatum res est rejecta,; and: rem ad senatum,: aliquid ad pontificum collegium,; so, rem ad pontifices, Ver. Flac. ap. : rem ad Hannibalem,; : tu hoc animo esse debes, ut nihil huc reicias,.—Of personal objects: legati ab senatu rejecti ad populum, deos rogaverunt, etc.,; so ; ; ; 39, 3.— Absol.: tribuni appellati ad senatum rejecerunt,; fin.—
With respect to time, to put off to a later period, to defer, postpone (Ciceronian): a Kal. Febr. legationes in Idus Febr. reiciebantur,: reliqua in mensem Januarium,: repente abs te in mensem Quintilem rejecti sumus,.— *
Reicere se aliquo, to fling one's self on a thing, i. e. apply one's self to it (very rare): crede mihi, Caesarem ... maximum beneficium te sibi dedisse judicaturum, si huc te reicis, Balb. ap. , A, § 1.

la:noun:reiectio.html:
rējectĭo, ōnis, f.
reicio
,
a throwing back, throwing away. *
Lit.: sanguinis,i. e. throwing up,; .—
Trop., a rejecting, re jection (so in good prose, esp. freq. in Cic.).
In gen.: selectio et item rejectio,: quod si civi Romano licet esse Gaditanum, sive exilio, sive postliminio, sive rejectione hujus civitatis,.—
In partic.
In jurid. lang., a challenging, rejection of a judge: judicum,; so . — Absol.: rejectione interpositā,; .—
Transf., in gen.: excutere, quicquid dici potest, et velut rejectione factā ad optimum pervenire,: eruditorum, praef. § 7.—
Rhet. t. t.
In alium, a shifting off from one's self to another, (al. trajectio; v. Orell. N. cr.); cited also in .—
= Gr. ἀποδίωξις,the setting aside of considerations which are not pertinent, Jul. Rufin. Schem. Lex. § 12.

la:adj:reiectaneus.html:
rējectānĕus, a, um, adj.
reicio
,
that is to be rejected, rejectable (a word formed by Cic. as a philosoph. t. t.): morbum, egestatem, dolorem non appello mala, sed si libet, rejectanea (as a transl. of the Stoic ἀποπροηγμένα), (cf. rejecta, ; and reicienda,; and reducta, q. v.).
